column4: Imran's wife says وَضَعَتْهَا and وَضَعْتُهَا أُنثَىٰ: the section's unloading/birth sense of وضع is enacted, while the girl's reception challenges the old formula that coupled easy birth with a boy.

After the girl's birth in 3:36, her Rabb accepts her well, causes her to grow وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا, and entrusts her to Zechariah; this gathers divine nurture, gradual growth, and human caregiving around the child whom the old curse devalued.
The pregnant women's term ends أَن يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ, and the same ayah promises the God-fearing person يُسْرًا in his affair, directly joining delivery of a carried load to divinely given ease.

The post-birth instruction provides housing and nursing, then says وَإِن تَعَاسَرْتُمْ another woman will nurse the child; it makes interpersonal difficulty part of the same delivery-and-care sequence as 65:4 and 65:7.

Within the birth and nursing passage, Allah limits burden to what He has given and promises سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا, the clearest parallel to the section's divine promise of ease around hardship.

حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ كُرْهًا وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهًا states both painful carrying and painful delivery, grounding the section's lexical meeting in a mother's bodily hardship and the child's later maturation.
At the Hour every nursing mother is distracted and every pregnant one تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا; the ordinary release of a carried child becomes an involuntary sign of overwhelming terror.
Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk; this supplies the concrete difficult-birth scene behind the source dictionary's عسر formula rather than merely sharing a word for hardship.
Pharaoh asks أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا, using the same “did we not … you” recollection as the surah while turning nurture into a boast against the person raised.
أَلَمْ يَجِدْكَ يَتِيمًا فَـَٔاوَىٰ recalls divine shelter in the same interrogative stance; unlike Pharaoh's reproach, the reminder places present strain inside a history of care.
No female وَمَا تَحْمِلُ مِنْ أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ except with God's knowledge, and measured life terms follow; carrying, delivery, hidden knowledge, and measure meet in one statement.
No fruit emerges and no female تَحْمِلُ مِنْ أُنثَىٰ وَلَا تَضَعُ except with God's knowledge, placing unseen gestation and its eventual disclosure under the same Lordly knowledge.
The wife first حَمَلَتْ حَمْلًا خَفِيفًا, then becomes heavy and the pair pray to their Rabb for a sound child; light load, increasing weight, birth hope, and dependence converge.
God knows مَا تَحْمِلُ كُلُّ أُنثَىٰ, what wombs diminish or increase, and gives everything a measure; it makes gestation a hidden, changing process held within exact measure.
A mother حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ وَهْنًا عَلَىٰ وَهْنٍ and weans over two years, extending the image from pregnancy's accumulating weakness into gradual post-birth care.
Mothers nurse for two complete years, fathers provide fairly, and no soul is burdened beyond capacity; the ayah joins nursing, completion, provision, and a limit on imposed weight.

The ayah follows human formation through womb stages, appointed term, birth, and maturity, then mirrors it in dead earth swelling and growing; it expands the section's gradual nurture and plant-growth metaphor.
God creates people خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ in three womb-darknesses and also sends down livestock in pairs; staged gestation, the Rabb, and the section's flock sense meet here.
Before the delivery in 3:36, Imran's wife dedicates مَا فِي بَطْنِي and asks God to accept it; the unborn child is already carried, entrusted, and oriented toward divine reception.
Immediately after seeing Mary's divinely supplied nurture in 3:37, Zechariah asks his Rabb for ذُرِّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً, so caregiving awakens a prayer for offspring rather than a preference for one sex.

After the promised boy, Zechariah is told وَٱذْكُر رَّبَّكَ كَثِيرًا; the passage places Qur'anic remembrance beside male offspring and thus exposes the distinct senses gathered under the section's ذكر root.
The casting of pens asks أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ, recalling how Mary's caregiver was chosen; it supplies the contested human guardianship behind 3:37's divine nurturing.
فَحَمَلَتْهُ begins Mary's pregnancy and withdrawal, giving the bodily carrying that culminates in the labor of 19:23.
At the point of labor, a call tells Mary not to grieve and announces a stream beneath her; the birth hardship is met from within by immediate reassurance and provision.
Mary returns to her people تَحْمِلُهُ, so حمل now names carrying the born child in her arms rather than carrying him in the womb, a precise shift within the same scene.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts; birth opens into the faculties by which a dependent child is gradually made capable.
God grants females to whom He wills and males to whom He wills, naming daughters first as divine gifts and directly reversing the old blessing that treated the boy as the fortunate result.
God may join male and female offspring or leave someone barren; sex and fertility are Lordly gifts and limits, not signs that difficult female birth is a curse.

The ayah places nursing mothers and sisters beside رَبَائِبُكُمْ, whose Qur'anic sense is stepdaughters rather than the source dictionary's “caretakers”; the same root-family neighborhood clarifies both child care and a semantic boundary.
Against the legal fiction of calling a wife “mother,” the ayah says mothers are only ٱلَّـٰٓـِٔي وَلَدْنَهُمْ; actual giving birth defines the bodily relation, while speech cannot manufacture it.
The deniers يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ, turning the section's definition of wizr as a heavy sin-load into a burden visibly borne on backs.
The messenger يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ and their shackles; this is the closest external enactment of the surah's placing-off of a crushing burden.

حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ ٱلْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا joins وضع and أوزار in the idiom “until war lays down its burdens,” sharply distinguishing war's equipment/weight from the personal sin-burden and childbirth senses.
The people say حُمِّلْنَا أَوْزَارًا of ornaments and then cast them away; a literal load is carried and unloaded, clarifying the physical metaphor inside moral وزر.
God tells the same prophetic addressee that He has given him from Himself ذِكْرًا; 20:100 then makes turning from this remembrance result in carrying a wizr.
Whoever turns from the revealed reminder فَإِنَّهُ يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَـٰمَةِ وِزْرًا, directly joining the section's ذكر and وزر roots through reception or refusal.
The burden of 20:100 is called a terrible حِمْلًا on resurrection day, making explicit that wizr is a carried load while keeping it distinct from pregnancy.

No burden-bearer bears another's burden, and even a مُثْقَلَةٌ calling for help with حِمْلِهَا transfers none of it; this sets the boundary around the surah's personally addressed burden and its removal.
The prayer asks the Rabb not to تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا or load people beyond their power, converting heavy-load language into an appeal for merciful measure and relief.
With the Rabb named at both ends, وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ fixes moral weight to its bearer; divine removal cannot be mistaken for shifting guilt to someone else.
وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ repeats the non-transfer rule and ties accountability to receiving a messenger, sharpening what kind of load the section's wizr is.
The repeated rule that no bearer carries another's wizr stands beside return to “your Rabb,” placing individual burden inside Lordly judgment rather than human transfer.
أَلَّا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ restates the boundary as part of the scriptures of Moses and Abraham, giving the section's burden a durable moral rule.
Those who mislead others carry their own أَوْزَارَهُمْ كَامِلَةً and part of others' burdens; the image of load is intensified by accumulation rather than relieved by transfer.
The disbelievers offer وَلْنَحْمِلْ خَطَايَاكُمْ, but the ayah denies that they can carry any of others' sins, exposing a false promise to take away another's moral load.
They will carry أَثْقَالَهُمْ وَأَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ, showing burdens added to burdens after 29:12 denies genuine transfer.
The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse to carry the Trust, while the human حَمَلَهَا; moral responsibility appears as an immense offered load, not a pregnancy.
يُرِيدُ ٱللَّهُ بِكُمُ ٱلْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ ٱلْعُسْرَ states divine intent as ease rather than hardship, a direct interpretive frame for the section's paired terms.
A debtor in عُسْرَةٍ receives time إِلَىٰ مَيْسَرَةٍ; material constriction is answered by patient room, making ease an ethical practice rather than only a future event.
وَسَنَقُولُ لَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِنَا يُسْرًا closely matches the promise of ease “in his affair” in 65:4, but in the setting of just rule over a believing person.
Moses prays رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي just before asking for ease; the child once raised in Pharaoh's house now seeks his Rabb's opening and preparation.
وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي is Moses' direct request that his Rabb make the mission easy, linking the Pharaoh upbringing scene to divinely prepared ease.
فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَـٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ joins divine easing and remembering in address to the Prophet, reuniting the section's يسر and ذكر roots in their Qur'anic senses.
وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِلذِّكْرِ makes ease serve remembrance, a direct Qur'anic meeting of the two roots that the section also brings together through birth vocabulary.
The repeated وَيَسَّرْنَا ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِلذِّكْرِ confirms that ease-for-remembrance is a refrain, not an isolated verbal coincidence.
The third refrain again makes the Qur'an easy for ذكر after a warning narrative, showing remembered revelation as the offered ease.
The fourth refrain completes the repeated association of تيسير with ذكر and invites an answering act of remembrance.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ is a divine “We–you” promise to prepare the addressee for ease, closely matching the surah's stance of recalled care and promised facility.
The oath by the creation of ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ precedes two opposed kinds of facilitation in 92:7 and 92:10; the surah relocates ease and hardship from a child's sex to a person's moral course.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ promises facilitation toward ease to the giving, God-fearing person, severing “easy” from the old preference for a male birth.
رَبِّ ٱرْحَمْهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا uses the Rabb root for parents' raising a small child and turns received nurture into a prayer for mercy toward the caregivers.
The Rabb preserves two orphans' treasure until they reach full strength; this is gradual protective nurture aimed at completion, exactly the section's definition of tarbiya enacted as providence.
The infant Moses is placed where Pharaoh's household will take him, yet God says وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي; his formation and care are claimed as divine even inside the human palace.
Moses' sister finds a carer, he is returned to his mother, rescued from distress, tested through stages, and arrives عَلَىٰ قَدَرٍ; the ayah compresses nursing, relief, formation, and measure.
Moses' mother is told to nurse him and promised both his return and future mission, joining immediate maternal care to a hidden divine plan for the child.
After wet nurses are barred to the infant, his sister offers a household that will يَكْفُلُونَهُ and care sincerely; this is the caregiver sense made into a concrete nursing search.
God restores Moses to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may know the promise true, turning separation into divinely arranged maternal nurture.
After sheltering the orphan in 93:6, God recalls finding the addressee in need of direction and guiding him; the remembered care advances in stages.
The sequence ends by recalling need and divine enrichment, completing the shelter–guidance–provision pattern of Rabb-like nurture.

The ayah names sheep and goats, males and females, and مَا ٱشْتَمَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ أَرْحَامُ ٱلْأُنثَيَيْنِ; it gathers the section's flock, womb, and sex distinctions while challenging invented gender rules.
Livestock تَحْمِلُ أَثْقَالَكُمْ to a land reachable only with severe strain, while “your Rabb” is compassionate; carrying a heavy load and merciful easing occupy one concrete scene.
At the cosmic upheaval, pregnant she-camels are abandoned; the most prized near-birth animals lose their ordinary care, pairing an animal gestation scene with 22:2's disrupted pregnancy.
The human drop is placed in قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ, a secure lodging, giving the carried child a protected hidden place before the stages of 23:14.
Successive transformations lead to ثُمَّ أَنشَأْنَـٰهُ خَلْقًا ءَاخَرَ, a Qur'anic picture of development stage by stage toward a completed new creature.
Creation proceeds from dust and a drop through a clot, birth as a child, maturity, and old age; this is the section's gradual bringing-to-completion across a whole life.
وَقَدْ خَلَقَكُمْ أَطْوَارًا states that people were created in stages, the most concise parallel to tarbiya as development حالًا فحالًا.
وَٱللَّهُ أَنۢبَتَكُم مِّنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا applies plant-growth language to people, directly echoing Mary's good growth in 3:37.
God forms people in the wombs however He wills; the hidden child is shaped under divine choice before any human valuation as male or female.
In a divorce context, women may not conceal what God created in their wombs; hidden pregnancy becomes legally consequential, preparing the more explicit delivery term in 65:4.
The repeated male/female pairs end with ٱلذَّاكِرِينَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرًا وَٱلذَّاكِرَاتِ, joining sex distinction to the remembrance sense of ذكر while giving both equal promise.
God creates the pair ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ, placing both sexes under one creative act rather than ranking the ease or worth of their births.
The male–female pair of 53:45 comes مِن نُّطْفَةٍ إِذَا تُمْنَىٰ, rooting sexual distinction in one shared generative origin.
After forming and proportioning the embryo, God makes مِنْهُ ٱلزَّوْجَيْنِ ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ; boy and girl are twin outcomes of the same measured making.
When one of them is given news of a female, his face darkens; this human reaction is the precise opposite of the Rabb's good acceptance of Mary.
The father hides from people and debates keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her, exposing the evil judgment behind the old female-birth curse.
The one given news of what he attributes to the Merciful becomes dark-faced and suppresses grief; the repeated daughter-announcement scene again opposes divine gift to human shame.
The buried infant girl is summoned and questioned, giving the devalued female child a public place in judgment that reverses her erasure at birth.
بِأَىِّ ذَنۢبٍ قُتِلَتْ denies that the newborn girl carried any guilt, a stark boundary between the section's sin-burden and violence inflicted on a female child.
God creates humanity from male and female, then makes taqwa—not sex—the measure of honor; this corrects the value judgment embedded in the old blessing and curse.
In the same surah as Mary's birth, God says He never wastes the work of male or female and بَعْضُكُم مِّنۢ بَعْضٍ, giving an explicit answer to gendered devaluation.
Moses answers Pharaoh's claimed favor by pointing to his enslavement of the Children of Israel; the human boast of raising one child is bounded by the oppression that made that upbringing possible.
Pharaoh slaughters sons and spares women while weakening a people; his later claim to have nurtured Moses is illuminated by the regime's destruction of other children.
The repeated memory of Pharaoh's people slaughtering sons and sparing women sets collective child-killing against his personal boast that he raised Moses.
This recurrence again names the slaughter of sons and survival of women as a severe trial, preventing Pharaoh's household nurture from being read apart from its violence.
Moses himself recalls deliverance from Pharaoh's slaughter of sons, a direct counter-memory to Pharaoh's self-serving recollection in 26:18.

The pagans reserve what is in livestock wombs for males and forbid it to wives, with another rule for stillbirth; condemned gendered claims over womb-content mirror the section's rejected valuation of sex.
The command not to kill children from fear of poverty is grounded in God's provision for them and their parents, opposing anxious destruction to Rabb-like provision after birth.
The parallel ban on killing children because of poverty says God provides for parents and children, again defining care and provision as the answer to fear around offspring.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ is a deliberately paradoxical facilitation toward hardship for the miser who denies; it relocates عسر from childbirth to a chosen moral trajectory.
كَلَّا لَا وَزَرَ uses وزر to mean a refuge, not a carried sin-load; the identical form marks a semantic boundary that guards the section's burden reading.
The angels announce Yahya to Zechariah while he stands praying, supplying the promised child immediately after his prayer awakened by Mary's care and provision.
Zechariah asks how he can have a boy in old age with a barren wife; bodily impossibility makes the child a gift of divine agency rather than the reward presumed by a birth formula.
Mary is told during labor to shake the palm so fresh dates fall; her own small action meets provision within the difficult birth scene.
“Eat, drink, and be comforted” completes the immediate care after labor, making bodily replenishment part of the transition from carrying to birth.
After the mother's painful carrying and delivery and the child's growth to forty in 46:15, God accepts the adult's best deeds and overlooks faults; human maturation culminates in divine acceptance.
Pharaoh's household picks up the exposed infant who will become their enemy, beginning the paradoxical human upbringing later claimed in 26:18.
Pharaoh's wife calls the infant a comfort and proposes taking him as a child; adoptive welcome inside a murderous regime complicates Pharaoh's later boast of nurture.
When Moses reaches maturity and full strength, God gives him judgment and knowledge, completing the staged development begun with his nursing and return to his mother.
Joseph's buyer proposes honoring his lodging or taking him as a child, while God is establishing him in the land; human adoption becomes one instrument of hidden nurture.
Just before the pregnancy ruling, the God-fearing person is promised a way out; this supplies the release-pattern in which 65:4's childbirth and ease are heard.
God provides from where the God-fearing person does not reckon and brings His purpose to completion, giving the provision and measure that frame 65:4's delivery rule.
Later in the same surah God says He has sent down to the believers ذِكْرًا, adding the remembrance root to the passage already joining pregnancy, difficulty, and ease.
Knowledge of what is in the wombs belongs to God among the hidden matters, reinforcing the section's movement from an unseen carried child to disclosed birth.
Human progeny is made from an extract of lowly fluid, supplying the humble beginning for the shaping and faculties of 32:9.
God proportions the human, breathes spirit, and gives hearing, sight, and hearts; the child is made fit in stages rather than merely delivered.
God knew people when they were أَجِنَّةٌ فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهَـٰتِكُمْ, so the hidden unborn stage becomes grounds for humility rather than claims of purity or worth.
The human begins as a drop of emitted fluid, initiating the measured formation that reaches male and female in 75:39.
The drop becomes a clot and God creates and proportions it, supplying the formative act immediately before the two sexes are named.
God creates the human from a mixed drop as a test and makes him hearing and seeing; generative origin leads into fitted capacities and responsibility.
The generative fluid is placed in قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ, portraying the womb as the secure place in which the load is held.
The hidden placement lasts إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍ مَّعْلُومٍ, an appointed measure that parallels the pregnancy term ending in delivery.
فَقَدَرْنَا فَنِعْمَ ٱلْقَـٰدِرُونَ attributes the gestational measure to divine determination, completing the secure-place sequence.
God creates the human from a drop and فَقَدَّرَهُ, providing conception and measure as the context for the possibly birth-related easing of the way in 80:20.
ٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ describes creating, proportioning, and balancing the person, a compact parallel to nurture toward fitness and completion.
God composes the person in whatever form He wills, placing final form under divine choice rather than under a hierarchy of desired birth outcomes.
The command to glorify the name of “your Rabb” opens the sequence that moves through creating, measuring, guiding, and easing in 87:2–8.
The Rabb خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ—creates and makes fit—giving a terse formulation of the section's gradual bringing to completion.
وَٱلَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ joins measure to guidance before the promise of easing in 87:8, making ease part of directed preparation.
فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ follows the promise of ease in 87:8, so facilitated mission issues in the act of reminding.
Zechariah tells his Rabb that his wife is barren and asks for an heir, placing hoped-for birth inside acknowledged human inability.
The answer announces a boy, Yahya, with a name not given before, presenting male offspring as a singular divine gift rather than a conventional sign of easy fortune.
Zechariah asks how a boy can come when his wife is barren and he has reached extreme old age, a repeated scene of hardship overcome by creation.
Zechariah prays to his Rabb not to leave him alone, expressing need for offspring without treating a child's sex as the measure of blessing.
God answers, grants Yahya, and وَأَصْلَحْنَا لَهُ زَوْجَهُ; the barren condition is made fit for birth through divine response.
Abraham's wife receives news of Isaac and then Jacob while standing nearby, a birth promise that includes generational continuation.
She asks أَأَلِدُ وَأَنَا۠ عَجُوزٌ with an aged husband, making bodily difficulty explicit in the voice of the prospective mother.
The messengers answer that God's mercy and blessings are upon the household, locating the extraordinary birth under the Rabb's care.
Abraham asks whether they give him birth tidings despite old age, another concrete boundary where apparent difficulty does not prevent the promised child.
The guests give Abraham news of a knowing boy, beginning the scene whose mother's barrenness is named in 51:29.
His wife approaches in astonishment and calls herself عَجُوزٌ عَقِيمٌ, making age and barrenness the stated obstacle to birth.
The messengers say “Thus has your Rabb said,” returning the unlikely birth to the wise, knowing Lord rather than to ordinary capacity.
Abraham asks his Rabb for a child among the righteous, another offspring prayer whose desired quality is righteousness rather than maleness as social prestige.
God gives him news of a forbearing boy; the birth promise answers 37:100 and begins a father-child sequence of growth and testing.
When the boy reaches the age of working alongside his father, the narrative marks gradual growth from promised child to capable companion.
Livestock are described as حَمُولَةً وَفَرْشًا, burden-bearing and smaller animals, giving the section's flock vocabulary a concrete spectrum of carrying capacity.
The next livestock pairs again ask whether males, females, or what wombs contain were forbidden, extending 6:143's challenge to invented sex distinctions.
Livestock bellies yield pure milk for drinkers, a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the source dictionary's secondary picture of a flock abundant in milk.
The livestock lesson again gives drink from their bellies and many benefits, grounding the section's flock-abundance sense in provided nourishment.
People have benefits and drinks from the herds God made for them; this corresponds to the source's milk-rich flock while making gratitude the proper response.
Livestock supply benefits and desired needs, and people are carried on them and ships; provision and load-bearing meet in one scene.
God makes mates among humans and livestock and multiplies them thereby, joining human offspring to the section's secondary sense of flock increase.
Humanity comes from one soul and its mate and spreads into many men and women, while the ayah closes by invoking womb-ties; sex, reproduction, and kinship share one origin.
God says He has made the revelation easy in the Prophet's tongue to give good news and warning, a second “We eased it for you” stance centered on communication.
Moses asks that forgetfulness not be held against him and that he not be burdened with difficulty in his affair, a human plea for room inside a demanding apprenticeship.
The messenger bears what he is charged with and the audience bears what it is charged with, using carrying for assigned responsibility and preserving the distinction between burdens.
One who shifts his own offense onto an innocent person has اِحْتَمَلَ بُهْتَـٰنًا وَإِثْمًا, showing that false transfer only adds a new carried sin.
Those who harm innocent believers اِحْتَمَلُوا بُهْتَـٰنًا وَإِثْمًا مُّبِينًا, another explicit moral use of carrying a nonphysical load.
God raises the sky and وَوَضَعَ ٱلْمِيزَانَ; raising and placing appear together, clarifying that وضع can establish something rather than unload or give birth.
Many creatures do not تَحْمِلُ رِزْقَهَا, yet God provides for them and for people; inability to carry one's provision becomes a reason for trust in the Provider.
The believers are likened to a crop that sends out shoots, strengthens, thickens, and stands upright, an extended staged-growth counterpart to Mary's being grown as a good plant.
ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ may include God's easing of the birth passage after the measured embryo in 80:19, though the “way” can also be read more broadly as life's or guidance's path.

When Zechariah asks how the promised boy can come, his Rabb answers that it is easy for Him and recalls creating Zechariah from nothing; divine ease directly answers apparent reproductive impossibility.

Mary's corresponding birth question receives the answer that it is easy for her Rabb, who will make the child a sign and mercy; this is a nonlexical but explicit promise of ease immediately before she carries him in 19:22.
Mary asks her Rabb how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer places the otherwise impossible birth under God's unrestricted creating and command.
Before recounting Moses' infancy, God says that He had already favored him another time; this divine reminder of nurturing favor is the direct counterpart to Pharaoh's self-serving reminder in 26:18.
The one who carries wrongdoing fails before the Living, Sustaining One; moral wrong is again made a carried load, with divine sustaining power as its setting.
God says He carried their offspring in the laden ship, joining descendants, divine carrying, and a vessel already bearing a load in one rescue image.
God honors the children of Adam, carries them on land and sea, and provides good things; carrying and provision become acts of continuing divine care for those once carried in wombs.
God recalls that when the water overflowed, “We carried you” in the vessel so the rescue would become a remembrance; divine carrying leads to survival and remembered care.
The girl accepted and grown in 3:36–37 is later told that God chose and purified her above the women of the worlds, a decisive reversal of the inherited shame attached to a female birth.
People count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, but God says that guidance is His favor to them; this distinguishes reproachful human favor-claiming from a truthful divine reminder of care.
Whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while believing enters the Garden without injustice; divine acceptance is explicitly independent of the sex privileged by the old birth formula.
In the same surah that depicts shame at a daughter's announcement, God promises a good life and full reward to any believing doer of good, male or female.
The believer promises entry into the Garden to every believing righteous person, male or female, replacing valuation by sex with valuation by faith and action.
Pharaoh orders the sons of those who believe with Moses killed and their women spared, another direct exposure of the violent regime behind his claim to have raised one boy.
The trumpet day is called a difficult day; its unrelieved eschatological hardship sets up the explicit denial of ease in 74:10, unlike the section's promise of ease with hardship.
The difficult day is “not easy” for the disbelievers, providing a precise boundary case where hardship is not accompanied by the ease promised to the addressed believer in the section.
Believers are told not to nullify charity by reproachful reminders and injury; this names what is wrong with Pharaoh's use of remembered upbringing as leverage.
The family of Imran is introduced as offspring, one from another, just before the pregnant woman's vow; the birth scene thus belongs to a continuing but divinely heard lineage.
The angels give Mary news of a child identified as the Messiah, initiating the promised-birth scene whose human impossibility she voices in 3:47.
The promised child will speak in the cradle and in maturity, placing infancy and completed growth side by side within Mary's announcement scene.
Mary asks how she can have a boy when no man has touched her and she has not been unchaste; her stated obstacle gives 19:21's declaration of divine ease its concrete birth context.
Mary guards her chastity, receives the breathed spirit, and confirms her Rabb's words; this compressed conception scene supplies the hidden beginning of the child later carried and born.
The parallel account says God breathed into the woman who guarded her chastity and made her and her son a sign, presenting mother and born child together under divine agency.
God makes Mary's son and his mother a sign and shelters them on secure high ground with rest and flowing water, extending the birth image into protective lodging and provision.
God recalls inspiring Moses' mother, making maternal action itself part of the hidden divine nurture elaborated in 20:39–40.
After losing the infant, Moses' mother's heart becomes empty and God strengthens it so she can remain faithful; maternal distress is held and made firm within the caregiving sequence.
Moses' mother sends his sister to follow him, supplying the family care that leads to the nursing solution in 28:12.
When Joseph reaches maturity, God gives him judgment and knowledge; the child whom a household considered adopting in 12:21 is shown brought to full capability.
God creates from weakness, brings strength after weakness, then weakness and gray hair after strength; the life cycle makes gradual formation and decline explicit.
Immediately after the livestock milk and benefits of 23:21, people are carried on the animals and on ships; nourishment and burden-bearing are consecutive provisions.
The donkey carrying books supplies a different kind of load: physical carriage without receiving or living the knowledge borne, sharpening the distinction between carrying and inward appropriation.
The oath invokes bearers carrying a load; although the bearers' identification is interpretively disputed, the ayah contributes the exact act of carrying weight before 51:3 invokes ease.
The next oath invokes those moving with ease, placing easy motion directly after load-bearing without specifying childbirth; the juxtaposition is a cautious indirect parallel to the section.
Giving and God-consciousness are the first conditions preceding facilitation toward ease in 92:7, showing what that ease answers in its own passage.
Affirming the best completes the positive stance before 92:7's promise, locating ease in moral response rather than in the sex of a birth.
Miserliness and self-sufficiency begin the contrary stance that culminates in facilitation toward hardship in 92:10.
Denying the best completes the negative stance before 92:10, clarifying that its hardship answers refusal rather than bodily childbirth.
God reminds people that He created cattle for them, supplying the herds to which the drinks and benefits of 36:73 belong.
The cattle are made manageable, with some serving as mounts and some as food; this gives the human use and control immediately before the herd's drinks are named.
God makes livestock for riding and eating, identifying the animals referred to when 40:80 adds benefits and being carried on them.
Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food, a broad but concrete picture of the useful abundance behind the section's milk-rich, fruitful flock sense.
Those who spend without following their gift by reproachful reminder or injury retain their reward; this supplies the positive boundary against Pharaoh's weaponized recollection of care.
